name: Industrial Nim
description: n quarries each produce an arithmetic run of pile sizes (x_i, x_i+1, ..., x_i+m_i-1); playing standard Nim over the union of all these piles, determine the winner under optimal play.
why_hard: With up to 10^5 ranges of up to 10^16 piles each, you cannot XOR piles individually — you must derive and apply the closed-form formula for the XOR of a full range of consecutive integers (based on the range length mod 4), then combine across ranges.

name: Thanos Nim
description: With n (even) piles, each move a player must choose exactly n/2 nonempty piles and remove any positive number of stones from each independently; the player who cannot move (fewer than n/2 nonempty piles remain) loses — determine the winner.
why_hard: The move rule breaks the standard XOR-of-piles Nim theory entirely; the actual winning condition is a slick parity argument on how many piles hold the current maximum value, which must be discovered rather than looked up.

name: Stair Game
description: Balls sit on n numbered stairs; a move takes any positive number of balls from a stair k != 1 down to stair k-1, and the player who moves last wins — determine the winner for a given starting configuration.
why_hard: This is the classic Staircase Nim reduction — the game is equivalent to ordinary Nim played only on the odd-numbered stairs (XOR of their ball counts), a non-obvious equivalence that must be proven and applied.

name: Not a Nim Problem
description: n piles of stones; a move removes y stones from a pile of size x only if gcd(x, y) = 1, and the player unable to move loses — determine the winner.
why_hard: The move restriction (only coprime removals allowed) means standard Nim XOR doesn't directly apply; you must compute the Grundy number of each pile size from its smallest prime factor structure and only then XOR them together.

name: Game of Stones
description: n independent piles (sizes up to 60); a move removes any positive number of stones from a pile, but the exact same removal amount can never be reused on that same pile again — determine the winner.
why_hard: The "no repeated move size per pile" constraint means a pile's Grundy number depends on its whole history of prior moves, not just its current size, requiring a bitmask/DP formulation of each pile's Grundy value before XOR-combining the independent games.

name: Mojtaba and Arpa's game
description: Given a list of numbers, a move picks a prime power p^k dividing at least one number, and divides every number in the list divisible by p^k by p^k; the player unable to move loses — determine the winner.
why_hard: Each number's prime factorization decomposes into independent per-prime subgames whose Grundy values must be derived from number-theoretic structure (exponent vectors), then combined via Sprague-Grundy XOR across primes and list elements — a genuinely layered application of the theorem.

name: Grundy's Game
description: A heap of n coins; a move splits one heap into two nonempty heaps of different sizes, and the player who makes the last possible move wins — determine the winner.
why_hard: Directly named for the theorem it teaches — computing the Grundy number of a heap requires recursively taking the mex over all ways to split it into two unequal heaps, the textbook mex/Grundy-number computation.

name: Nim Game II
subtopic: Combinatorial Game Sums & Misère Play (Sprague-Grundy sum of games)
description: With n heaps of sticks where a move removes 1, 2, or 3 sticks from one heap, and the player who removes the last stick wins, determine the winner under optimal play.
why_hard: Each heap is a distinct subtraction game whose Grundy value (x mod 4) must first be computed independently, then the Sprague-Grundy theorem combines them via XOR — a direct test of the "sum of independent games" principle beyond plain Nim, where the per-heap game itself isn't standard Nim.

name: Another Game
subtopic: Combinatorial Game Sums & Misère Play (non-XOR game sum)
description: With n heaps of coins where a move selects any subset of nonempty heaps and removes one coin from each, and the player who removes the last coin wins, determine the winner under optimal play.
why_hard: This move rule (remove from many heaps simultaneously) is not standard Nim and the naive Sprague-Grundy XOR-of-piles rule does not directly apply; the correct analysis works bit-by-bit across the binary representations of the heap sizes, testing whether the solver understands the limits of the basic Nim-sum shortcut and can derive the right combination rule from first principles.

name: Plate Game
description: Two players alternately place a circular plate of the same fixed radius on an a x b rectangular table, plates may not overlap and must lie entirely within the table; the player who cannot place another plate loses — determine the winner.
why_hard: The board is continuous, not a discrete grid, so there's no finite state space to search; the winner is settled by a symmetry-stealing argument — if one plate fits at all, the first player places it exactly at the table's center and then mirrors every later move of the opponent through that center, which guarantees a legal reply forever.

name: 1-2-K Game
description: A chip starts on cell n of a strip numbered 0 to n; each move shifts it left by exactly 1, 2, or k cells without going below 0, and the player who cannot move loses — answer many independent (n, k) queries for the winner.
why_hard: The plain subtraction game with moves {1, 2} has clean period-3 losing positions, but throwing in the extra move k can either fold into that period or create its own; you must case-split on k mod 3 (with a special mod (k+1) correction when k mod 3 == 0) to get the right closed-form winner, since neither case reduces to a single simple formula.

name: Stoned Game
description: n piles of stones; players alternately remove exactly one stone from a nonempty pile, but may not pick the pile the opponent just picked on the immediately preceding turn (the first move is unrestricted) — the player unable to choose a pile loses.
why_hard: There's no XOR/Grundy structure to exploit here; the winner is decided by comparing the largest pile to the sum of the rest — if it strictly exceeds that sum the first player wins by relentlessly attacking it, and otherwise the whole game collapses to just the parity of the total stone count, a two-case result that has to be proven via an exchange argument rather than computed directly.

name: A Lot of Games
description: Two players play the standard build-a-common-prefix word game (on a trie of n given strings) k times in a row; the loser of game i moves first in game i+1, and the overall winner is whoever wins the k-th game — determine the outcome of the whole match under optimal play.
why_hard: Winning each individual game is not the goal — a player may need to deliberately lose an early game just to seize the first move later, so the real task is a two-flag DP over the trie (can-force-a-win, can-force-a-loss from this node) that lets you determine, for any starting mover, whether they can force any outcome they like across the sequence of k games.

name: Fox and Card Game
description: n piles of cards; on each turn a player takes one card from the top of any nonempty pile (Ciel) or the bottom of any nonempty pile (Jiro), each trying to maximize their own total — compute both players' optimal final scores.
why_hard: Minimax over the real move tree is infeasible; the actual solution sorts each pile and gives Ciel the top half by value and Jiro the bottom half, but odd-sized piles each leave one 'middle' card behind — those middles get pooled into a single shared array that both players then draft greedily in turn — and proving this reduction is optimal (not just simulating it) is the real content of the problem.
